title: 1 Samuel 17:41–54
context: This is the heart of the chapter, kept here as one unit. Goliath despises David and curses him by his gods. David answers that he comes in the name of the LORD of Armies, and that the LORD will deliver the Philistine into his hand so that all the earth may know there is a God in Israel and that the battle is the LORD’s. A single stone fells Goliath, and David finishes him with Goliath’s own sword. Israel routs the Philistines. Two questions are often raised. Verse 50 says David killed Goliath with sling and stone without a sword, and verse 51 says he killed him with the sword; some read verse 50 as a summary that anticipates verse 51, others take the stone as the decisive blow that the sword completes, and others see two strands of tradition. Separately, WEB’s 2 Samuel 21:19 reads that Elhanan killed “Goliath the Gittite’s brother,” and 1 Chronicles 20:5 names that brother Lahmi. The traditional Hebrew of 2 Samuel 21:19 lacks “brother” and reads as Elhanan killing Goliath the Gittite; this edition of the WEB has no footnote on the verse. Proposals include copying damage in 2 Samuel, a second warrior of the same name, or differing traditions. Many Christians in both traditions also see in David’s victory a pattern fulfilled in Christ, while cautioning that David’s courage is also a call to faith, not only an allegory. Both traditions build on the shared ground of verses 45–47: faith in the living God, who saves without sword and spear.

verses.text: The Philistine walked and came near to David; and the man who bore the shield went before him.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistine advances toward David, with his shield bearer in front of him. The two champions now approach each other.

Arminian readers note that Goliath comes with full protection while David comes with only a sling, so the reader sees the contrast between self-reliance and trust in God embodied in the two figures.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the scene is carefully staged to display that the outcome will depend on the LORD, since every visible advantage lies with the Philistine and his shield bearer.

This verse is commonly listed among those lacking in the shorter Septuagint form. Both traditions read the approach as the climax of the contrast that the chapter has been building between human might and faith in God.

verses.text: When the Philistine looked around and saw David, he disdained him; for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and had a good looking face.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the Philistine sees David, he despises him, because he is only a youth, ruddy and good-looking. Goliath judges by appearance.

Arminian readers note that Goliath’s contempt shows the blindness of pride, which dismisses others by outward appearance and fails to consider the God who stands behind them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the irony that a similar description of David’s appearance (16:12) accompanied his anointing, where God looked beyond appearance to the heart, while Goliath sees only appearance and despises.

Both traditions read the verse as exposing the folly of judging by sight rather than by God’s choice.

verses.text: The Philistine said to David, “Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?” The Philistine cursed David by his gods.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistine asks David whether he is a dog that David comes to him with sticks, and curses David by his gods. The insult becomes religious.

Arminian readers note that the cursing by his gods makes the contest explicitly a confrontation between the living God and the gods of the Philistines, as in the ark narrative with Dagon (5:1–5).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Goliath invokes his gods against the LORD’s anointed, so the battle that follows will vindicate the LORD as the only true God over the nations.

Both traditions see the curse as turning the duel into a demonstration of whose God is real, and both note that Goliath mistakes David’s staff for his weapon.

verses.text: The Philistine said to David, “Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and to the animals of the field.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistine tells David to come, and he will give his flesh to the birds of the sky and the animals of the field. He threatens a shameful death without burial.

Arminian readers note that Goliath’s boast is complete confidence in his own strength, the very attitude Scripture warns precedes a fall (Proverbs 16:18).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David will turn this very threat back on the Philistine army in verse 46, showing that God reverses the boasts of the proud and brings their words upon their own heads.

Both traditions see the threat as setting up God’s reversal of the arrogant.

verses.text: Then David said to the Philistine, “You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of the LORD of Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.
verses.arminianNotes:
David answers that Goliath comes with sword, spear and javelin, but he comes “in the name of the LORD of Armies”, the God of Israel’s armies whom Goliath has defied. This is David’s central confession.

Arminian readers note that David freely and publicly stakes everything on the LORD’s name, a decision of faith that every believer is invited to make when facing what seems impossible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the name of the LORD represents God’s revealed character and covenant power, so David’s confidence rests entirely on who God is and what he has promised, not on David’s ability.

Both traditions hold this verse as shared ground: true strength is found in the name of the LORD.

verses.text: Today, the LORD will deliver you into my hand. I will strike you and take your head from off you. I will give the dead bodies of the army of the Philistines today to the birds of the sky and to the wild animals of the earth, that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel,
verses.arminianNotes:
David declares that the LORD will deliver Goliath into his hand that day, that he will strike him and cut off his head, and that the Philistine dead will feed the birds and wild animals, so that all the earth may know “that there is a God in Israel”.

Arminian readers note the universal aim: God acts so that all nations may know him, reflecting his desire that people everywhere come to know the true God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s ultimate purpose is the display of his own glory before the nations, and that David’s victory serves that purpose rather than David’s fame.

Both traditions agree that the battle’s goal is the knowledge of the true God among all peoples.

verses.text: and that all this assembly may know that the LORD doesn’t save with sword and spear; for the battle is the LORD’s, and he will give you into our hand.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David adds that the assembly will know that the LORD does not save with sword and spear, for “the battle is the LORD’s”, and he will give the Philistines into Israel’s hand.

Arminian readers note that this truth calls for active trust: David still fights, but he understands that the outcome depends on God, which is the posture of faith God asks of all his people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that salvation belongs to the LORD, not to human weapons, and that God works through David’s hand while remaining the true author of the victory.

Both traditions treat this verse as foundational shared ground: the LORD saves, and his people respond with faithful action, though they explain the relation between God’s working and human effort in somewhat different terms.

verses.text: When the Philistine arose, and walked and came near to meet David, David hurried and ran toward the army to meet the Philistine.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the Philistine moves toward him, David hurries and runs toward the battle line to meet him. David does not hesitate.

Arminian readers note that David’s running toward the enemy shows faith expressed in decisive action; trust in God does not make him passive but energizes his response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the one whom God has chosen runs toward the danger that sent all Israel fleeing (17:24), showing that the courage the army lacked has been given to God’s anointed servant.

Both traditions see David’s running as faith in motion, and both recognize that some scholars list part of this verse among the material lacking in the shorter Septuagint form.

verses.text: David put his hand in his bag, took a stone and slung it, and struck the Philistine in his forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
David takes a stone from his bag, slings it, and strikes the Philistine in the forehead, so that the stone sinks in and Goliath falls on his face. One stone settles the contest.

Arminian readers note that David’s skill with the sling, developed through faithful practice as a shepherd, is the means God uses; human ability and divine help work together.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Goliath falls on his face to the earth, recalling Dagon fallen on his face before the ark (5:3–4), and that God governs even the flight of a stone, displaying his sovereign control over small details.

Both traditions credit the LORD with the victory and honor David’s faithful skill.

verses.text: So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck the Philistine and killed him; but there was no sword in David’s hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
So David prevails over the Philistine with sling and stone, striking and killing him, though no sword is in his hand. The verse emphasizes the absence of a sword.

Arminian readers note that some interpreters read this verse as a summary that anticipates the detail of verse 51, while others see the stone as the decisive blow that the sword then completes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that others see two strands of tradition joined here, and that this verse is also commonly listed among those lacking in the shorter Septuagint form; these views are held with humility, and none needs to be declared final.

Both traditions agree that the verse stresses that victory came without the weapons Goliath trusted.

verses.text: Then David ran, stood over the Philistine, took his sword, drew it out of its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.
verses.arminianNotes:
David runs, stands over the Philistine, draws Goliath’s own sword, kills him and cuts off his head, and the Philistines flee when they see their champion dead. The giant’s weapon completes his defeat.

Arminian readers note that David takes decisive action to finish the victory, and that faith brings tasks to completion rather than leaving them half done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the irony that Goliath’s own sword, the emblem of his strength, becomes the instrument of his death, a fitting picture of how God turns the weapons of the proud against them (compare Psalm 7:15–16).

Both traditions note the reversal, and both see the Philistines’ flight as breaking the terms Goliath himself had set (17:9).

verses.text: The men of Israel and of Judah arose and shouted, and pursued the Philistines as far as Gai and to the gates of Ekron. The wounded of the Philistines fell down by the way to Shaaraim, even to Gath and to Ekron.
verses.arminianNotes:
The men of Israel and Judah rise up, shout and pursue the Philistines as far as Gai and the gates of Ekron, and the wounded fall along the road to Shaaraim, Gath and Ekron. The whole army is now emboldened.

Arminian readers note that one person’s faith stirs others to courage, and that the army’s renewed boldness shows how faithful example can change a community’s response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the people who fled in fear now pursue in confidence, not because they changed by themselves but because God’s victory through his anointed has given them courage. Gai means valley in Hebrew, and some ancient versions read Gath instead.

Both traditions see the rout as the fruit of God’s victory.

verses.text: The children of Israel returned from chasing after the Philistines, and they plundered their camp.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Israelites return from chasing the Philistines and plunder their camp. The victory brings material gain.

Arminian readers note that God’s people share in the benefits of a victory they did not win themselves, which invites gratitude rather than pride, and calls them to remember who gave the triumph.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the plunder is a gift following a deliverance God accomplished through one man, and that Israel’s part is to receive what has been won and give thanks.

Many Christians in both traditions see an analogy here to receiving the benefits of Christ’s victory, while remembering that the verse is first a historical report and that David’s example also calls each reader to courageous faith.

verses.text: David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, but he put his armor in his tent.
verses.arminianNotes:
David brings Goliath’s head to Jerusalem but puts his armor in his tent. Jerusalem was not yet in Israel’s control (2 Samuel 5:6–9), so interpreters debate whether this notes a later act or anticipates the city’s future.

Arminian readers note that the narrator may be telling the story from a later vantage, and that the detail need not be harmonized with certainty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that proposals include a later display of the head after David took the city, or a general statement of where the trophy eventually went; the text does not settle it. Goliath’s sword later appears at Nob (21:9).

Both traditions handle the detail with care and agree it does not affect the chapter’s message.
